html:
In the year 1000, or possibly 999, the Althing, Iceland's general assembly, voted to make Christianity the law of the land. Icelanders call it kristnitakan, "the taking of Christianity".

Most of the people who came in the settlement of Iceland worshipped the Norse gods. Missionaries from the 980s had little success, and Olaf Tryggvason, the Christian king of Norway, added pressure by holding Icelanders in Norway as hostages. At the Althing the Christian and pagan parties came close to fighting and seemed ready to split into two peoples with two laws.

They agreed to let the lawspeaker Thorgeir, a pagan, decide. He is said to have lain under his cloak for a day and a night before he spoke. His ruling was that all must be baptised and the island must keep one law, but that people could still sacrifice to the old gods in private, eat horse meat and leave unwanted infants to die. These exceptions were dropped a few years later.

The story is told in the Book of the Icelanders by Ari the Learned. Christianity brought writing in Latin letters, which later made possible the sagas and the work of Snorri Sturluson.
